## Introduction

PaleoClimR reads HadCM3L NetCDF files, as formatted by the BRIDGE group at the 
University of Bristol (for further details see 
<https://www.paleo.bristol.ac.uk/ummodel/scripts/papers/Using_BRIDGE_webpages.pdf>). 
HadCM3L is a lower-resolution configuration of the Hadley Centre Coupled Model 
version 3 (HadCM3); the package's functions for it are prefixed `HADCM3.`.
This vignette demonstrates these functions for inspecting grids, extracting 2D
and 3D data, mapping fields, plotting transects, and matching palaeogeographic
occurrence points.

The package includes a reduced HadCM3L example file containing the
`insitu_T_ym_dpth` temperature field and the coordinates needed to interpret
its grid. It contains one saved timestep. The simulation (`tfkSy`)
represents the late Permian at 252 Ma.
The cGENIE output in the companion vignette is directly related to this HADCM3 output, so 
plate configurations are consistent. The PBDB example contains broadly coeval
Changhsingian occurrences. The file was contributed by Dan Lunt (University of
Bristol); see Judd et al. (2024) for further details on this and related
HadCM3L simulations.

```{r example-file}
hadcm3_exp_path <- PaleoClimR.example("HADCM3.permian.example")
hadcm3_file <- "tfkSy_252o.pgclann"
```

## Using your own files

The HADCM3 functions all take a `file` and an `experiment` argument. `file` is
the NetCDF file name without the `.nc` extension, and `experiment` is the
directory that contains it. To work with your own BRIDGE-formatted output,
replace the example values used throughout this vignette with your own, for
example:

```{r own-data, eval = FALSE}
hadcm3_grid <- HADCM3.grid(
  file = "your_file_prefix",          # without .nc
  experiment = "path/to/your/directory",
  dims = 3
)
```

## Inspecting grid and NetCDF data

`HADCM3.grid()` returns longitude, latitude, and cell-edge coordinates. With
`dims = 3`, it also returns the model depth levels and depth edges.

```{r grid}
hadcm3_grid <- HADCM3.grid(
  file = hadcm3_file,
  experiment = hadcm3_exp_path,
  dims = 3
)

names(hadcm3_grid)

c(
  longitude_cells = length(hadcm3_grid$lon),
  latitude_cells = length(hadcm3_grid$lat),
  depth_levels = length(hadcm3_grid$depth)
)
```

The example grid therefore has `r length(hadcm3_grid$lon)` longitude cells,
`r length(hadcm3_grid$lat)` latitude cells and `r length(hadcm3_grid$depth)`
depth levels.

`HADCM3.get.nc()` reads the requested field and returns a list containing the
field as an array (`var`), together with the grid coordinates and time value.

```{r get-netcdf}
temperature_nc <- HADCM3.get.nc(
  var = "insitu_T_ym_dpth",
  file = hadcm3_file,
  experiment = hadcm3_exp_path
)

names(temperature_nc)

dim(temperature_nc$var)
```

## Extracting 2D and 3D data

`HADCM3.data()` extracts one horizontal depth slice and returns a data frame
with cell bounds and a `var` column. In this example, depth level 1 is the
shallowest level. Land cells have `NA` values, so they are dropped before
printing the first rows, and `summary()` reports how many there are.

```{r data-2d}
temperature_surface <- HADCM3.data(
  var = "insitu_T_ym_dpth",
  file = hadcm3_file,
  experiment = hadcm3_exp_path,
  depth.level = 1
)

head(temperature_surface[!is.na(temperature_surface$var), ])

summary(temperature_surface$var)
```

`HADCM3.data.3D()` returns the field across all model depths, with the depth
midpoint and bounds included for each grid cell.

```{r data-3d}
temperature_3d <- HADCM3.data.3D(
  var = "insitu_T_ym_dpth",
  file = hadcm3_file,
  experiment = hadcm3_exp_path
)

dim(temperature_3d)

head(temperature_3d[!is.na(temperature_3d$var), ])
```

## Mapping HADCM3 fields

`HADCM3.map()` maps a selected depth level. The bundled temperature values are
in degrees Celsius, and this example displays a
colour range of -4 to 36 °C.

```{r map}
HADCM3.map(
  var = "insitu_T_ym_dpth",
  file = hadcm3_file,
  experiment = hadcm3_exp_path,
  depth.level = 1,
  unit.factor = 1,
  min.value = -4,
  max.value = 36,
  intervals = 4,
  scale.label = "Temperature (\u00B0C)"
)
```

## Creating transect plots

`HADCM3.transect()` extracts the nearest latitude or longitude band and plots
the field against depth. Setting `orientation = "lon"` draws a longitude–depth
section along a fixed latitude, set by `degrees`, so `degrees = 0` selects the
latitude band nearest the equator. Setting `continents.outlined = TRUE` adds an
outline marking the continents along the section.

```{r transect}
HADCM3.transect(
  var = "insitu_T_ym_dpth",
  file = hadcm3_file,
  experiment = hadcm3_exp_path,
  degrees = 0,
  orientation = "lon",
  continents.outlined = TRUE,
  unit.factor = 1,
  min.value = -4,
  max.value = 36,
  intervals = 4,
  scale.label = "Temperature (\u00B0C)"
)
```

## Matching palaeogeographic points

The bundled `PBDB.permian.example` data include palaeogeographic coordinates
in `p_lng` and `p_lat`, which were generated with the PALEOMAP plate model of
Scotese. The HadCM3L simulation uses the same plate model family, so the occurrences
and the model grid share a consistent palaeogeography.
`HADCM3.points.data()` matches each occurrence to the model grid cell it falls
in, and returns the matched climate value and model grid coordinates with the
original occurrence records. Occurrences that fall in a cell with no data (for
example, where a palaeocoastline in the plate model and the coarse model
land–sea mask disagree) receive an `NA` matched value.

```{r points-data}
data("PBDB.permian.example", package = "PaleoClimR")

matched_occurrences <- HADCM3.points.data(
  var = "insitu_T_ym_dpth",
  file = hadcm3_file,
  experiment = hadcm3_exp_path,
  depth.level = 1,
  coord.dat = PBDB.permian.example
)

head(matched_occurrences[, c(
  "p_lng", "p_lat", "matched_climate", "lon.bin.mid", "lat.bin.mid"
)])

sum(is.na(matched_occurrences$matched_climate))
```

In this example, `r sum(is.na(matched_occurrences$matched_climate))` of
`r nrow(matched_occurrences)` occurrences fall in cells with no data.

`HADCM3.points.map()` overlays those matched records on the map. The example
uses phylum for a separate categorical point-colour scale; omit `points.col`
to colour points using their matched temperature instead.

```{r points-map}
HADCM3.points.map(
  var = "insitu_T_ym_dpth",
  file = hadcm3_file,
  experiment = hadcm3_exp_path,
  depth.level = 1,
  coord.dat = PBDB.permian.example,
  unit.factor = 1,
  min.value = -4,
  max.value = 36,
  intervals = 4,
  scale.label = "Temperature (\u00B0C)",
  points.col = "phylum",
  points.scale.type = "categorical",
  points.scale.label = "Phylum"
)
```

## Summary

The core HADCM3 workflow that is expected to be useful to general users is
to identify a file and experiment directory, inspect the grid with `HADCM3.grid()` 
if needed, extract data with `HADCM3.data()` or `HADCM3.data.3D()`, and visualise it 
with `HADCM3.map()` or `HADCM3.transect()`. Use the point functions to associate 
(already rotated) palaeogeographic occurrences with model values and plot the 
matched records.
